Uti enim ad virtutem superanda natura, ita etiam ad scientiam omnino certam motus omnis temporis ac ævi: quo spectet illud Hesych. Περιοριστόν, περίγραπτον: nec apte Turr. terminans ac definiens. Τὸ ἐνώσεως: plane mendum est, pro γνώσεως: cui uni etiam congruit epithetum ἀπλανοῦς. et quæ contra ἀρετὴν ubique Maximo aliisque distinguitur; scientia scilicet, non unitio vel conjunctio. The Scholiast best reveals Maximus's meaning.

Stultum enim est deliberare de his quæ non sunt in nostra facultate: non autem simplici appetitu ex phantasia ac cogitando ea velle, motu potius brutis affine, quam ex ratione. The occasion of the gap was the repetition of 'τῶν ἐφ' ἡμῖν', than which nothing is easier, so that something is omitted.

Aliis cogitatum, sensus, prudentia, intelligentia, sapientia; sic enim etiam φρονεῖν, sapere: quandoque etiam animus et appetitus. Quam hic Maximus harum vocum proprietatem observat, auctores liberiore earum usu fere negligunt. Quod definit Maximus, φρόνησιν, id est prudentiam, ἕξιν ἀνοίας καὶ ὑπερνοίας ἀντίπαλον: non bene reddit Turr. sive ejus cod. habuit ἀγνοίας, sive fefellit oculus, aut mens præcurrit, Ignorantiæ adversariam, imo, mentis inopiæ, dementiæ, imprudentiæ per defectum; uti ὑπερνοίας, per excessum, quam sufficientiam, dicere possimus; vitium scilicet ὑψινοίᾳ affine, id est superbiæ; qua quis eximie et supra reliquos putat se sapere.

unplaced.en: On φρόνημα (mindset). Cicero too has trouble rendering this word. Others render it: thought, sense, prudence, intelligence, wisdom; so also φρονεῖν, to be wise; sometimes also mind and appetite. How carefully Maximus observes the proper sense of these words, while authors almost neglect them in their freer usage. Maximus defines φρόνησις, that is prudence, as 'a state opposed to folly and to over-wisdom': Turrianus (or his codex, which had ἀγνοίας; or his eye failed, or his mind ran ahead) does not render it well as 'opposed to ignorance'; rather, 'to poverty of mind, madness, imprudence by defect', as ὑπερνοία (over-wisdom), by excess, we may call self-sufficiency; a vice akin to ὑψινοία, that is, pride, by which one thinks oneself exceptionally wise and above the rest.

unplaced.en: ... of the guilt of sin, and brought upon the whole human race from Adam's transgression; which Maximus, in that question 24, explains as 'the other sin', which Christ was made, in Pauline phrase: namely the passible element (to pathēton) of nature, free of any guilt, by which he also procured incorruption and immortality for us; Damascene and others call them 'blameless passions', from which the faith teaches that Christ was voluntarily liable. Turrianus, otherwise learned, does not do well with 'passions of our honesty'; nor has he everywhere grasped the finely balanced words of so theological a man as Maximus. The word ἐπιτίμια is known even to beginners, especially in ecclesiastical matters. So the Greeks commonly call all ecclesiastical penalties, what we call censures, with a clever play on words: 'what belongs to penalty' and 'what belongs to dishonour', which in Latin are 'penalty and guilt'. Christ first assumed the one, and by it healed the other (which he also claimed as his own), and removed the nature of it; whereby he has given us a pledge of the following natural incorruption, he has given a pledge of the incorruption that follows and accompanies those penalties in Christ: which is the very renewal of nature, thus celebrated by Maximus, Nyssen, Damascene and other Greek Fathers; namely the rectitude of nature, as it was established in Adam, going first in Christ as in the head, and to come in us as in his members; of which we too have the pledge in him. Nor did Turrianus do well to make it, by his office, a pledge of natural immortality; which Christ did not assume, but its contrary, the passible element of the flesh, its power of suffering and dying; borrowed from guilty Adam for this one thing, to repair in us his other, namely his original rectitude, which is his natural incorruption; the supreme immunity from everything that has grown in us from sin.

unplaced.en: Chapter 50. So Dufresne's codex gives it in abbreviated form, which is the sign of the fiftieth chapter of that work which Maximus wrote to Marinus the priest; and so, from the Roman codices, Lucas Holstenius rightly wrote 'chapter fiftieth'. But Turrianus's codex (perhaps itself a copy received from the most reverend Gerasimus Blachus), in rendering κεφάλαια πεντήκοντα as 'fifty chapters', acts as a rather inaccurate interpreter, to whom even so the plain error did not occur. For who would imagine 'fifty chapters' here, not the fiftieth alone, which is immediately followed by the fifty-first, the two of that great labour of Maximus that survive for us? 'To the same Marinus' (Πρὸς τὸν αὐτὸν Μαρῖνον) is found in one Blachus codex alone. And that so great a work of Maximus to Marinus has perished, about which there can be no doubt, with only this and one other ear of so great a sheaf surviving to us in these 'collectanea', what wonder that the letter too has perished in which he excuses himself to the same Marinus about the diploma sent from Rome by the pope to Constantinople, so that it exists nowhere entire but only as excerpts, reported here and there by those who wrote on the procession of the Spirit, defending or attacking the argument of the Latins, so that even Catholic men draw a quite frivolous argument from it, as if it were understood to be a question of spuriousness, when otherwise it has Maximus's scholastic characteristics, and is not lacking in the testimony of the ancients, given Maximus's date. I am more astonished that Cardinal Baronius thinks this work, distinguished by fifty chapters, to be the very letter to Marinus which stands here first among those edited by Gretser from Turrianus's version, though that scarcely exceeds twelve chapters; after which follows that chapter 51 from the said work on the operations and wills. Obviously the size of the work prevented the illustrious writer from consulting the book; otherwise he would have deserved very well of the church, had he found the work entire and at least pointed it out.

Stulta religiositas sic scribæ festinantis manu in præceps agi, ut vel cum luce clarior aberratio est, ipseque perspicuus auctoris sensus, emendare nolis, ac vel indicare quod emendandum videris.

Turrianus's rendering of the 'union of coeval parts, forced' (synodon enagkasmenen) as 'coactam' does not please me: true philosophy admits nothing forced (what common usage calls violent) in natural things; such is that conjunction of the parts, or rather their coming-together (coitus), as the Greek word sounds, by which a kind of mutual natural inclination seems to be meant. That conjunction is therefore necessary, since it is not sought by will but follows from the very inclination of nature (the action of the efficient cause being supposed); it is not itself forced or violent.

Ἄνωθεν ergo, ipsum est quod ἀπ' ἀρχῆς, a principio, ex ipsa origine ac processione; quomodo usurpavit Greg. in hoc carmine, Ὧν τὸ μὲν ἦεν ἄνωθεν· Quorum hoc quidem erat a principio, ex origine; uti etiam Demosth. τὸ συνουσιωμένην, secundum substantiam unitam; longe est a viro theologo. συνουσιασμός, Eutychianorum est et Severianorum; unitio secundum substantiam, et substantialis, sive etiam naturalis, Christi Ecclesiæ, auctore præsertim Cyrillo. Illud, substantiarum confusio, altera ab altera absorpta, vel etiam ex ambabus una tertia effecta, uti passim Maximus exprimit, et qui eam confundentium hæresim impugnant: istud, vera essentiarum seu naturarum, καθ' ὑπόστασιν, sustinendi ratione (quæ et post unitionem distinctionem retineant, ac quod unaquæque nata est) copulatio. Nec in re sic trita morandum, nisi quantum adegit tanta illa superioris interpretis vere ἀθεόλογος; oscitantia.
unplaced.anchorLine: …συνουσιωμένην αὐτῷ (n) κατενέχθη…
unplaced.en: 'But from above and from the beginning united in substance with him.' Turrianus has: 'But bringing it from above and from the beginning he joined it to himself according to substance', as though these words supported the one error of Valentinus, of a body brought down from heaven and of heavenly matter, not taken from us; which is utterly far from Maximus's mind. That ἄνωθεν must be taken as here [rendered] is shown by Maximus's own correction, 'or not having taken', which Turrianus did not lack either when he renders 'or did not take'. He certainly took it, even if he brought it down from above, that is from heaven. So ἄνωθεν is the same as ἀπ' ἀρχῆς, 'from the beginning', from the very origin and procession, as Gregory uses it in his poem, 'of which one was from above', that is 'from the beginning, from the origin'; so too Demosthenes. The word συνουσιωμένην, 'united in substance', is far from the theologian. συνουσιασμός belongs to the Eutychians and Severians: a union according to substance, and substantial or even natural, of Christ and the Church, especially according to Cyril. The one [sense] is a confusion of substances, one swallowed by the other, or even a third made from both, as Maximus everywhere expresses it and as those who oppose the heresy of the confounders do; the other is a union of true essences or natures, according to hypostasis, on the principle of sustaining them (which retain their distinction even after the union, and what each was born to be). One need not linger over so well-worn a matter, except so far as that great carelessness of the earlier translator, truly lacking sound theology, compelled it.

unplaced.text: Καλοφροσύνης. Vox paulo rarior. Hesych. τὸ καλόφρον affert, explicanda voce εὔφρων, uti etiam vocem αἰδέσιμος: huncque vel maxime ejus sensum putem hic spectasse Maximum, prout vox αἰδέσιμος active etiam sumitur; quam ejus significationem confirmavi ex Orig. in ejus Catena in Genesim, ubi illi sermo est de Rebecca. Catena hæc exiguis laboribus undecunque licuit ex omnibus Origenianis in Scripturam mihi collecta, notisque illustrata, in Huetii manibus prælum exspectat: nec quia symbolæ sunt, sic elevandæ, ut jam vir doctus insinuavit. Videmus quanta fide in aliis excerptæ ejusmodi symbolæ, ipsoque adeo Origene, in quibus libri integri exstant, ut inde libros aliquot Cyrilli in Joannem supplere licuerit. Breviant plerumque, quandoque etiam, servata sententia, tantisper verba mutant, qui hoc scribendi genus, inter Græcos maxime, secuti sunt: quo fit ut in secundis habenda sint ejus generis scripta, non ut pene nulla; mihi haud raro interpolatis Rufino ejusque affusis furfuribus ad fidem auctorumque censum potiora. Sed hæc obiter. Ad rem quod attinet, prætexebant pietatem Eutychiani et Monothelitæ, quasi vererentur illi quidem, nec admissa distinctione solveretur naturarum unitio; hi vero, ne contrarias in Christo voluntates ac peccatum inducerent, si et humana præditum voluntate dicerent. Quæ maxime Sergii cavillatio fuit, ejusque discipuli Macarii Antiocheni. Reddi itaque possit, animi probitas, verecundia ac pudor, cautio ac timor, et si quid ejusmodi est: Turr. bellam prudentiam reddit: possit et sapientiam. Dictum καλοφροσύνης, quasi ironice et per ἀντίφρασιν, pro κακοφροσύνης, quod est malitia, mentis, perversitas.
unplaced.anchorLine: σύνης (p), ταύτην τινὲς προφασίζονται· καὶ τὸν
unplaced.en: 'Καλοφροσύνης': a somewhat rare word. Hesychius offers τὸ καλόφρον, explained by the word εὔφρων, as also the word αἰδέσιμος; and I think Maximus had chiefly this sense in view here, as αἰδέσιμος is also taken actively; I confirmed that meaning from Origen in his Catena on Genesis, where he speaks of Rebecca. This Catena, gathered by me with modest labour from all the Origenian material on Scripture wherever possible, and annotated, awaits the press in Huet's hands; nor, because they are mere excerpts, should they be belittled, as a learned man has already hinted. We see with what fidelity such excerpts were made elsewhere, even from Origen himself, where whole books survive, so that several books of Cyril on John could be supplied from them. Those who follow this kind of writing, chiefly among the Greeks, often abridge and sometimes, keeping the sense, change the wording for a while; so such writings are to be counted second-rank, not as nearly worthless; to me they are often preferable to texts interpolated by Rufinus and sprinkled with his chaff, as regards faithfulness and the weight of authors. But that is by the way. As to the point at hand: the Eutychians and Monothelites put forward piety as a pretext, as if they feared that, once a distinction was admitted, the union of the natures would be dissolved; and the latter, lest they introduce contrary wills in Christ and sin, if they said he was endowed with a human will as well. This was above all the quibble of Sergius and of his disciple Macarius of Antioch. It can therefore be rendered 'uprightness of mind, modesty and shame, caution and fear', and whatever is of that kind; Turrianus renders it 'bellam prudentiam' ['fine prudence']; 'wisdom' also could be used. [The Greek] was said of καλοφροσύνη as if ironically and by antiphrasis, for κακοφροσύνη, that is malice, malignity of mind, perversity.

Ac certe carnis Christi communitatem hanc operationis ac virtutis cum Verbo ac unitione ad ipsum, nedum in propria specie, sed et in mystica benedictione, ut vocat, seu Eucharistia, nemo Patrum plenius Cyrillo altiusque exsecutus est, prorsus consentanee ac proxime Dionysio, sive ipsum Cyrillus legit, sive eamdem ac ille ecclesiasticam doctrinam ac traditionem exposuit: cujus etiam multa mihi relata ac stylo ornata in Biblioth. PP. concionat. ad diem festum Corporis Christi. Non satis expedite Turr., maximam sententiam Patris continet.
unplaced.anchorLine: τούτου Πατρὸς μεγίστης ἔχεται διανοίας (q).
unplaced.en: 'Holds to a very great thought.' It coheres with the understanding of Dionysius; it has the same most exalted sense. And certainly, as to this communion of Christ's flesh in operation and power with the Word and by union with him, not only in its proper kind but also in 'mystical blessing', as he calls it, that is the Eucharist, no Father has treated it more fully and more deeply than Cyril, in complete agreement and closest accord with Dionysius, whether Cyril read Dionysius himself or set out the same ecclesiastical doctrine and tradition as he; many of Cyril's words on this I have reported, adorned with style, in the Bibliotheca Patrum, in the sermon for the feast of Corpus Christi. Turrianus renders it not very clearly; it contains the Father's greatest thought.

Durum mihi, carne philosophari de cœlestibus et æternis; de rebus scilicet ævi futuri. Hæc enim sunt τὰ ἐκεῖ, ut et τὰ ἐνταῦθα, quæ sunt ævi præsentis. Spiritu potius et animo de illo philosophamur, etsi cum carne, illaque ei socia ac subministra, seu instrumento ejus philosophiæ; qua ipsa virtutibus componitur, ac ratione regitur.

Turrianus has 'by which he philosophised about the things that are there'. It is hard for me [to accept] philosophising with the flesh about heavenly and eternal things, that is, about the things of the age to come. For these are τὰ ἐκεῖ ('the things there'), as τὰ ἐνταῦθα are 'the things here', which belong to the present age. We philosophise about it rather with spirit and mind, even if with the flesh, which is its companion and servant, or the instrument of that philosophy; and the flesh itself is ordered by the virtues and governed by reason.

unplaced.text: Ἀλλ' ἀμέτοχος πάντῃ. Legit Turr. ἀλλὰ μέτοχος, quod et habuit Geras. Blacchi cod. Venet. aperto nimis errore. Reddit itaque, sed potius participans omnino secundum substantiam ab omni natura differt. Quæ ipsa aperte pugnant. Non enim differt natura a natura, seu ab ea distinguitur, quod participet, sed quod non participet, sitque quo participent personæ et ὑποστάσεις, ipsa non participans. Quo fit ut, si una Christus natura est, uti operatio, nihil sit eorum ex quibus constitutus est, id est, nec Deus, nec homo, nec cum Patre nec nobiscum communicet. Quod argumentum, uti alibi passim, sic hic quoque Maximus vexat: nec debuit vir theologus re tam proclivi ab ejus deviare sententia, ac quod ab omni abhorret sacra profanaque philosophia, ex nota elisionis male omissa, festinante Antiquarii calamo, deroquere.
unplaced.anchorLine: ἀλλ' ἀμέτοχος, πάντῃ (t) κατ' οὐσίαν πρὸς πάσας
unplaced.en: 'But wholly without participation.' Turrianus read ἀλλὰ μέτοχος, 'but participating', which Geras also had, and the Venice codex of Blacchus, by an obvious error. So he renders it, 'but rather participating, wholly according to substance, it differs from every nature'. These things plainly contradict one another. For one nature does not differ from another, or is not distinguished from it, because it participates, but because it does not participate, and it is that in which persons and hypostases participate, itself not participating. Hence, if Christ is one nature, like his operation, he is none of the things from which he is composed, that is, he would be neither God nor man, and would not communicate with the Father or with us. This argument Maximus presses, as elsewhere throughout; the theologian should not have departed from his own meaning in so easy a matter, and from what every sound sacred or profane philosophy abhors, by an omitted elision-mark, [owing to] the hasty pen of the copyist, [to] ...  [the last word, 'deroquere', is unclear in the scan].

unplaced.text: Ἵν' ἐκ τούτου οὐ μεσίτας Θεοῦ μᾶλλον. Addidi negantem particulam, quod necessario sensus exposcit. Quid enim sensus, quod absque illa habent Græca, et reddit Turr. ut hinc vos magis sequestros Dei, quam imitatores præstetis. Imo certe contrarium. Significat enim episcopos pro munere, et qua divinis dotibus eo sublimes fulgent, non tam ad Deum intercedere (quanquam et hoc eorum muneris est) quam ipsos quoque (quod pene divinius videatur) Dei imitatione divina præbere ac perficere; quippe gradu ipso τελειωτικούς, sub summo hierarcha Christo, ea functione ejusque vicarios. Hoc enim est quod sequitur, Non solum ejus in omnem illustrationem ac misericordiam habitu consecuti ἀλλὰ καὶ ἄξια παρέχοντες: verum etiam pro dignitatis munere præbentes. Ubi Turr. ἄξια legit, sed digna etiam ei præbentes: male vero τὸ, ei, quasi eos digna Deo præbere dicat Maximus, quod prorsus abhorret, vel si ἄξια demus eum scripsisse. Præbent certe illi populis ἄξια, in hoc illis comparata dignitate; vel etiam ἄξια, ut quisque dignus est accipere. Sed illud primum longe aptius. Continere habitu, vel ea habitu nactos esse, privatorum potius est. Scripserit et ipse Turr. eis, etsi ita illi prelum erravit.
unplaced.anchorLine: διόρθωσιν· Ἵν' ἐκ τούτου μεσίτας Θεοῦ μᾶλλον (u),
unplaced.en: 'So that from this you may be mediators of God rather [than ...]'. I have added the negating particle, which the sense necessarily demands. For what sense is there, since the Greek has it without that, and Turrianus renders it 'that from this you may show yourselves rather as God's go-betweens than as imitators'? On the contrary, surely. For [Maximus] means that bishops, by their office and by the divine gifts by which they shine on high, do not so much intercede with God (though that too is part of their office) as also (which may seem almost more divine) bring about and perfect divine things in others by imitation of God, being in that very rank 'perfecters' under Christ the supreme hierarch, and his vicars in that function. For this is what follows: 'having attained not only the state of illumination and mercy that belongs to him, but also supplying worthy things'; indeed supplying them according to the dignity of their office. Where Turrianus reads ἄξια, but [translates] 'supplying worthy things to him': the 'to him' is wrong, as if Maximus said they supply God with worthy things, which he utterly rejects, even if we grant that he wrote ἄξια. They certainly supply the peoples with ἄξια, a dignity suited to them in this; or else ἄξια, as each is worthy to receive. But the first sense is far more apt. 'Containing by a habit', or 'having obtained them by a habit', is more characteristic of private persons. Turrianus himself may have written 'to them', even if the press erred so.

Sicque animo insinuat in prooemio. Titulus quem repræsentat Turr. Epistola sancti Maximi ad sanctos Patres præpositos et monachos, et populos catholicos insulæ Siciliæ habitatores, contra eos qui unam in Christo operationem ponunt, ab Antiquario palam adjectus est; quem ex aliis repræsento, ipsa sit Maximo apposita ἐπιγραφή: magis proinde probanda; uti etiam quam repræsento ex Dufrenii Codice ad Quæst. in Scripturam.

unplaced.en: [The pronoun] seems to indicate a letter written in Sicily itself, when the Monothelites had already sought that refuge for themselves, so as to posit both one and two operations in Christ: which they tried to attribute to Maximus, and afterwards to drag him into it at the time of his first exile, when even Eugenius's apocrisiaries were led into that new faith. So Maximus seems to have wished that the Sicilians should have this as a sure pledge of his unblemished faith, and set it against all his detractors, since in it there was no such freedom for quibbling as in what he had said to them by word of mouth. And so he hints in the preface. The title Turrianus gives, 'Letter of Saint Maximus to the holy Fathers, superiors and monks, and the Catholic peoples inhabiting the island of Sicily, against those who posit one operation in Christ', was openly added by a copyist; the one I give from others is the very inscription attached by Maximus, and so is the more to be approved; as is also the one I give from the Dufresne codex of the Questions on Scripture.

unplaced.text: Τῶν ἀντιῤῥόπων καὶ ἐναντίων δογμάτων ὑπόληψις. Sic Maximus novam Monothelitarum opinionem argute vocat, seu illorum damnatæ jam hæresis commentum et evasionem. Una itaque voluntate et operatione, una cum Ecthesi, Joanni IV ac cunctis Occident. necnon Sophronio Hierosolymorum episcopo, reprobata, hoc novatoribus succurrit, ut tanquam ἀντίῤῥοπον (æquivalens, par, æquale) unam, duasque eas dicerent: quod tamen Maximus contrarium esse contendit; ac ejusmodi, ut alterum alterum evertat. Non recte itaque Turr. Nunquam me sensisse aut suspicatum esse de contrariis et repugnantibus dogmatibus, ut et infra, περὶ τῶν ἀντιῤῥόπων οὑτωσὶ καὶ ἐναντίων δογμάτων: de contrariis dogmatibus: ac si ambæ voces essent ejusdem prorsus significationis; quod longe est a vera Gramm. ἀντίῤῥοπον enim, ἰσόῤῥοπον est Suid. ἴσον, ἰσόσταθμον, ἰσόζυγον Hesych. quod perinde lancem trahit, ejusdemque ponderis est; a quo certe procul contrarii ratio est. Nec ii vero longe abesse a Monothelitarum illo genio videantur, qui nuper damnatarum Romæ propositionum acrius defensores, ac cum suo antistite, parum Thomistarum scholæ faventes, atque errantium albo, primo ipso ordine ascribentes, nunc sibi in uno Thoma, velut ei semper militaverint, præsidium quærunt: ac utinam vere quærant, ac quidquid de gratia senserint, ad illius normam, hinc plane erroris ac notæ perpetuo securi, componant. Ineptiunt enim, ni vere ἀσεβοῦντας quis malit dicere, nec magis Angelico præceptori quam ipsi Sedi apostolicæ, inque ea nuper præsidenti Alexandro VII injurii sunt, qui vel scioli vel procaces, vel invidi ac malevoli, obtinente ejus ipsius testimonio, damnatam sancti Thomæ ac Thomistarum in Jansenianam doctrinam deblaterant, aut etiam chartis illinunt atque evulgant.
unplaced.anchorLine: δογμάτων ὑπόληψις (x). Οὐδὲ γὰρ μίαν ἐν ταὐτῷ
unplaced.en: 'The supposition of counterbalancing and contrary doctrines.' So Maximus cleverly names the new opinion of the Monothelites, that is, the contrivance and evasion of their already condemned heresy. With one will and one operation rejected, together with the Ecthesis, by John IV and all the West, and by Sophronius, bishop of Jerusalem, this expedient helped the innovators: that they might say 'one' and 'two' of them as though ἀντίῤῥοπον ('equivalent, equal, level'); which Maximus nevertheless contends is contrary, and of such a kind that the one overturns the other. So Turrianus is wrong in 'that I never thought or suspected of contrary and conflicting doctrines', as also below, 'on the ἀντίῤῥοπα, thus and contrary doctrines': as if the two words had the same meaning, which is far from true grammar. For ἀντίῤῥοπον is the same as ἰσόῤῥοπον, Suidas; 'equal, of equal weight, equally yoked', Hesychius: it tips the scale just alike and is of the same weight; the idea of contrary is far from it. Nor do those seem to stand far from that Monothelite temper who, as recent vehement defenders of the propositions condemned at Rome, and little favouring the school of the Thomists, enrol themselves in the list of the erring in the very first rank, and now seek protection in Thomas alone, as though they had always served under him: would that they did truly seek it, and bring whatever they think about grace into line with his norm, thus safe for ever from error and censure. For they talk nonsense, unless one would rather call them truly impious, and they wrong the Angelic Doctor no more than the Apostolic See itself, and in it Alexander VII, then presiding, they who, whether smatterers or insolent or envious and spiteful, with his own testimony in their favour, babble about the condemned doctrine of St Thomas and the Thomists against the Jansenist doctrine, or even smear it on pages and publish it.

unplaced.text: Φύσιν τε λέγω καὶ ὑπόστασιν. Istud, quod superioris explicatio est, τοῦ καθ' ἑκατέραν, secundum utramque naturam scilicet et personam; Turr. velut absolutum facit relatum ad ὑπογράφοντες;, quo mihi ejus propositio non ferenda videtur, dum sic scribit, quasi Maximi sententiam reddens. Describentes, inquam, Filium esse naturam et hypostasim, quod est ab Ecclesia alienum. Ego non sic didici, nec me docuit Maximus; imo hunc Ecclesiæ catholicæ sensum accepi: nulla enim naturæ et hypostasis in Filio opposi io, ut non Catholice utrumque dici debeat, etsi idem duntaxat ratione naturæ cum Patre communicet, non ratione personæ; unumque hoc alienum dicat Maximus ab Ecclesia catholica, id est, cum eo communicare ratione utriusque, quod est personalem amborum oppositionem, ac proinde distinctionem, Sabelliano errore, tollere. Sic pronum in theologia, ex verbis incaute prolatis, in hæresim incidere, aut certe hæreticam pro Catholica propositionem dare.
unplaced.anchorLine: νοῦντα, φύσιν τε λέγω καὶ ὑπόστασιν (y), τὸν Υἱὸν
unplaced.en: 'I say nature and hypostasis.' This, which is an explanation of the preceding, [is of] τοῦ καθ' ἑκατέραν, that is 'according to each, nature and person'; Turrianus makes it as if absolute, relating it to ὑπογράφοντες, so that his proposition seems to me intolerable when he writes thus, as though rendering Maximus's meaning: 'Describing, I say, the Son to be nature and hypostasis', which is foreign to the Church. I did not learn it so, nor did Maximus teach me; on the contrary I took this to be the sense of the Catholic Church: for there is no opposition of nature and hypostasis in the Son, such that each could not be said in a Catholic way, although he communicates with the Father only in respect of nature, not of person; and the one thing Maximus calls foreign to the Catholic Church is to communicate with him in respect of both, which is to remove, by the Sabellian error, the personal opposition of the two and hence the distinction. So it is easy in theology to fall into heresy from incautiously uttered words, or at least to give a heretical proposition for a Catholic one.

Nam quæ exempla ponit Maximus, τὴν ἀνάστασιν, τὴν ἀνάληψιν: resurrectionem in cœlum receptionem, secundum ejus verum et planum sensum, ipsa vere divina signa et miracula, non εἰς ἄλλους exhibita dici possint in alios; bene tamen εἰς ἀνθρώπους, in homines: nam et ipse vere homo Salvator Deus, sic virtute divinitatis sanci-tatus, ut Paulus testis est, et in cœlum levatus. Qui de aliorum suscitatione et curatione exponeret (nam et ἀνάληψις probatis auctoribus et grammaticis θεραπεία est, et ἀνάρρωσις) nihil quidem is peccaret retinendo εἰς ἄλλους, quod et mihi primum placuerat: sed id durius-culum, et remotius a Maximi ecclesiastica styli simplicitate, qua libenter sacris ipsis ac receptis vocibus utatur: alias proclive admodum mutari τὸ ἀνοῦς breviatum, quod est, ἀνθρώπους, in ἄλλους

unplaced.text: (b) Ἐξουσιαστικὸς ὑπάρχων, καὶ τῆς τῶν ἁπάντων ἐξουσίας δημιουργός. Ex Dei nativa libertate, suique juris potestate, et quod ejusdem in naturis intelligentibus potestatis auctor ipse sit, recte suadet Maximus, non factum fuisse ἄνουν ἄνθρωπον, hominem mente destitutum; quæ ejus liberæ suique juris potestatis, principium est. Non bene itaque Turr. habens potestatem secundum naturam, et auctor substantiæ omnium; nempe pro ἐξουσίας, legens οὐσίας: quod nec sic ita ejus habuit cod., sic fuit dec[…]dum, ἐξουσιαστής, inter nomina Christi habetur Isa. ix, 6, quod tamen cum aliis a LXX positis, sanctus Hieronymus non exponit. Ejus loco reliqui interpret. δυνατὸς habent. Sonat maxime in potestatem illam, qua quis vel sibi ipse, vel aliis dominatur ac præcipit. Sic ἐξουσιαστικὰ verba appellantur, ἄρχω, κυριεύω, βασιλεύω, et quæ sunt ejus generis. Hinc τὸ αὐτεξούσιον, quod nostri vocant Liberum arbitrium, facultatem scilicet rationis sui dominæ, ac se moventis ex præconcepto fine.
unplaced.anchorLine: τῆς τῶν ἁπάντων ἐξουσίας δημιουργὸς (b), οὐκ ἄνους γέγονεν ἄνθρωπος
unplaced.en: ‘Having authority (ἐξουσιαστικός), and maker of the authority of all things.’ From God’s native freedom and his power over his own right, and from the fact that he himself is the author of that same power in intelligent natures, Maximus rightly argues that there was not made an ἄνους ἄνθρωπος, a man bereft of mind; for this is the principle of his free power over his own right. Turrianus therefore does not do well [to render] ‘having power according to nature, and author of the substance of all things’; that is, reading οὐσίας in place of ἐξουσίας; which his codex did not have in that form, so it had to be [dec…dum — word broken in print; probably ‘toned down’]: ἐξουσιαστής is counted among the names of Christ at Isa. 9:6, which however, with the other words set down by the LXX, St Jerome does not explain. In its place the other interpreters have δυνατός. It sounds especially of that power by which a person rules and commands either himself or others. So the verbs ἄρχω, κυριεύω, βασιλεύω and those of that kind are called ἐξουσιαστικά. Hence τὸ αὐτεξούσιον, which our writers call free will, [that is] the faculty of reason as its own mistress, moving itself from a preconceived end.

Non videtur supposita hæc epistola ad Marinum, aliqua esse ex illis quæ ad eum exstant, omnes dogmaticæ: ipsaque prima inter editos Turriano tractatus, serio γνωμικὴν in Christo impugnat voluntatem, et electionem nobis similem, solum admittens quatenus est motus liber, non tamen secundum contraria, aut conjunctam incerti rationem habens; sicque se admisisse Quæst. ad Thalass. excusat ac profitetur. Ubi quoque voluntatem κατ᾽ οἰκείωσιν, per arrogantiam et appropriationem ex Patrum sensu, ipsam nostram voluntatem, quam velut caput membrorum, suam quodammodo ducit, recte exponit; cui nihil commune cum tertia illa Monothelitarum voluntate ut totius, etsi eam etiam illi dicerent κατ᾽ οἰκείωσιν. Quæ seorsum exstat a reliquis Maximi epistolis ejus ad Marinum epistola, qua satisfacit pro adjecta particula Filioque Litteris apostolicis, num ejusmodi aliquid habuerit incertum est, cum nec illi qui Maximo abrogant, ejus quidquam insimulaverint. vel exemplum illius magis integrum, quam modo habeamus, nacti sint. Potuit sic ab iis Græcis ablegari, qui Phòtiani dogmatis studiosiores, Maximi piam illam expositionem ejusque εἰρηνικὸν non probaverunt.

unplaced.en: On ‘the one to Marinus’ (Τῆς πρὸς Μαρῖνον). This letter to Marinus does not seem to be spurious, [but] to be some one of those which survive addressed to him, all of them dogmatic; and the first of them, among those printed by Turrianus, seriously opposes a gnomic will (γνωμικήν) in Christ, and an election like ours, admitting it only so far as it is a free motion, yet not one according to contraries, nor having the conjoined notion of uncertainty; and so he excuses and professes that he admitted it in the Questions to Thalassius. Where also he rightly explains the will ‘by appropriation’ (κατ᾽ οἰκείωσιν), by arrogation and appropriation in the sense of the Fathers, [as] our own will, which he in a manner counts his own, as the head of the members; with which that third will of the Monothelites, [a will] of the whole, has nothing in common, even if they too called it κατ᾽ οἰκείωσιν. As to the letter to Marinus that stands apart from Maximus’s other letters, in which he gives satisfaction about the particle Filioque added to the apostolic letters, whether it contained anything of that kind is uncertain, since not even those who deny it to Maximus have charged him with anything. Or [they] may have obtained a copy of it more complete than the one we now have. It could thus have been got rid of by those Greeks who, more zealous for the Photian teaching, did not approve Maximus’s pious exposition and his peaceable statement (εἰρηνικόν).

Maximi locum ex epistola ad Marinum, de processione Spiritus ex Patre et Filio in Martini primi synodicis, quo offensi sint Constantinopolitani, ipseque Maximus exposuerit, ut non duas causas, sed unam, Patrem, Latini sentiant; nonnulli, etiam Catholici, an sit Maximi addubitant; vereorque ne Leo Allatius liberalior sit, in Vindiciis synodi Ephesinæ Cyrilli ea de re, cap. 72, cum ait plerosque addubitare. Anastasius in Collectaneis ut certæ fidei retulit, ac momentum habere in rem fidei et Ecclesiæ existimavit. In concilio Lugdunensi Gregorio X pontifice, nescio qui dubitarint: non Beccus, non Georgius Metochita, etc. In Florentino ea Maximi distinctione et sententia, Ecclesiarum pax conciliata: non Blemidas aliique Catholici ex schismaticis, Palamas, Marcus Ephesius, etc. Libri antiquissimi servarunt, in quibus codex ille Romanus antiquior vii synodo, ex quo exscriptus Reg. Michaele Duca Angelo Comneno imper. Qui dubitent, parum versatos in Maximi lectione existimo, nec ullam arbitror exstare ejus epistolam aut tomum dogmaticum, in quo ejus styli character clarius eluceat, quibus præsertim præfatur, ut in aliis ad eumdem Marinum dogmaticis, aliosque viros sacros, diversi argumenti epistolis. Nec sic a vero et catholico sensu abhorret Maximi expressio, ut tam facile ejus relinquendum vadimonium viro catholico sit. Una causa Pater absolute, seu auctor: nec Filius auctor, nisi quia a Patre, et ejus quasi virtus, quo cum una causa, et principium de principio: quod Græci libentius particula per exprimunt, ut ordinem significent, et Patri τὸ προκαταρκτικόν, ratione primæ causæ et originalis (a se scilicet) servent. Operæ pretium igitur fecit Maximus, qui et vivus, et vita functus, dissentaneas in specie Doctorum voces Virorumque Ecclesiasticorum eodem sensu, velut olim Athanasius in eadem prope materia (ac περὶ Θεολογίας) commiserit.
Locum Maximi eo ipso sensu egregie exponit Joan. Veccus, orat. 2, t. II Græciæ orth. p. 63 et 64, ubi omissa fusiori explicatione, quam Damasceno malit impendere, cujus causa difficilior, et quo adversarii magis glorientur, sic paucis de Maximo: Ὑμῖν δὲ οὐκ ἀγαπητὸν τῷ μεγάλῳ Μαξίμῳ κατακολουθεῖν ὑπερηγορούντι Ῥωμαίων, ἐφ᾽ οἷς καὶ τότε ἐκ Πατρὸς καὶ Υἱοῦ τὸ Πνεῦμα ἔλεγον ἐκπορεύεσθαι· καὶ οὐδὲν διαφέρειν, τὸ ἐκ Πατρὸς δι᾽ Υἱοῦ πρὸς τὸ, ἐξ ἀμφοῖν ἐκδιδάσκοντι· δι᾽ ὧν ἡ ἐπιστολὴ τὸ, ἐκ τοῦ Υἱοῦ ἐκπορεύεσθαι, εἰς τὸ, δι᾽ Υἱοῦ προϊέναι σαφῶς ἐκλαμβάνεται; Ubi Leo All. An non volupe vobis fuerit, magnum Maximum sequi, patrocinium Romanorum suscipientem, qui tum ex Patre et Filio Spiritum procedere affirmabant: nihilque differre ex Patre per Filium, et ex utroque, edocentem: quibus in illa epistola, Ex Filio procedere, in illud, Per Filium procedere, assumitur. Omissa Allatio particula καὶ, ipsa non inutilis, qua significatur esse hoc argumento antiquæ traditioni, cum nulla Ecclesiarum scissione sic Romana Ecclesia doceret, nec Græcam lateret. Vexatque egregie hoc argumentum Georgius Metochita in suis de processione Spiritus sancti quinque libris, a me ipsi Leoni Allatio transmissis, ut in tertium suæ Græciæ orthodoxæ volumen conferret; sicque transmissi tum mihi periere, tum rei ecclesiasticæ. Extrema verba 74 sic redderem: Ea ratione quod epistola, ex Filio procedere, palam exponat, ut sit idem ac per Filium prodire. Fuse vero idem ad Constantinum, l. iv, p. 203 et seq., ubi optime quasi utrique parti de processione Spiritus sancti studentem sanctum Maximum, molliendo illa verba junxisse, ut ad assensum traheret, rixamque sedaret: Ἐξ ὧν οὐκ αἰτίαν τοῦ Πνεύματος τὸν Υἱὸν ποιοῦντας σφᾶς ἑαυτοὺς ἀπέδειξαν. Ostenderunt se non causam Spiritus Filium facere: qualem illi sibi videbantur ex ipsorum verbis et modo profitendi, habere: primam scilicet, et qualis est Pater: quod ipsum illis ex contentione provenerat, et quod Latini Monothelitarum hæresis causa ipsos perstringerent; ut optime idem Veccus, p. 47, dicens se deprehendisse ex Maximi epistola; ac facile quisque advertat: nec aliter in Photio et Cerulario, sic privata odia vertentibus in causam fidei.
In excerpto, ex epistola quam Regius Cod. laudatus Romæ scriptam dicit, Romanus alter, qui solus habet, cum epistola ad Marinum conjungit, quasi sit illius pars: καὶ μεθ᾽ ἕτερα· quomodo non Romæ,
unplaced.en: [On] the passage of Maximus from the letter to Marinus, about the procession of the Spirit from the Father and the Son, in the synodical letters of Martin I, by which the Constantinopolitans were offended, and which Maximus himself explained so that the Latins hold not two causes but one, the Father: some, even Catholics, doubt whether it is Maximus’s; and I fear that Leo Allatius is rather too liberal, in his Vindication of the Synod of Ephesus of Cyril [Vindiciis synodi Ephesinæ Cyrilli], ch. 72, when he says that most doubt it [plerosque addubitare]. Anastasius in his Collectanea reported it as a matter of certain faith, and judged that it has weight for the faith and the Church. At the Council of Lyons under Pope Gregory X, I do not know who doubted it: not Beccus, not George Metochites, etc. At Florence, by that distinction and judgment of Maximus the peace of the Churches was made: not Blemmydes and other Catholics from the schismatics, [nor] Palamas, Mark of Ephesus, etc. [as printed: ‘non Blemidas aliique Catholici ex schismaticis, Palamas, Marcus Ephesius’]. The most ancient books preserved it, among them that Roman codex older than the Seventh Synod, from which the Regius [codex] was copied under the emperor Michael Doukas Angelos Komnenos. Those who doubt, I judge to be little versed in the reading of Maximus, and I think there exists no letter or dogmatic tome of his in which the character of his style shines out more clearly, especially in those [passages] where he prefaces, as in the other dogmatic letters to the same Marinus, and in letters of different content to other holy men. Nor does Maximus’s expression so far depart from the true and Catholic sense that a Catholic should so easily abandon the pledge [to it]. One cause: the Father absolutely, or author; the Son is not author except in that he is from the Father, and as his power, with which he is one cause, and a principle from a principle; which the Greeks more willingly express by the particle ‘through’, to signify order, and to preserve for the Father the προκαταρκτικόν (‘originating’), by reason of first and original cause (that is, from himself). Maximus therefore did well, who, alive and having ended his life, brought together in one sense voices that in appearance disagree, of Doctors and of Ecclesiastical men, as Athanasius did once on nearly the same subject (also on theology). John Veccus, Oration 2, vol. II of his Græcia orthodoxa, pp. 63 and 64, explains Maximus’s passage splendidly in that very sense, where, omitting a fuller explanation, which he prefers to give to Damascene, whose case is harder and over which the adversaries boast more, he says briefly of Maximus: [Greek, quoted:] ‘It is not agreeable to you to follow the great Maximus, who speaks up for the Romans, on account of which they then said that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son; and that there is no difference between “from the Father through the Son” and “from both”, teaching; by which the letter’s “to proceed from the Son” is clearly taken as “to go forth through the Son”?’ [my rendering of the Greek, which is partly broken in print]. Here Leo Allatius [says]: ‘Would it not please you to follow the great Maximus, who undertakes the defence of the Romans, who then affirmed that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son: and teaches that there is no difference between from the Father through the Son and from both: in which letter “to proceed from the Son” is taken up into “to proceed through the Son”.’ Allatius omits the particle καί, itself not useless, by which it is shown that this is an argument from ancient tradition, since the Roman Church taught so with no division of the Churches, and it was not hidden from the Greek [Church]. George Metochites vigorously presses this argument in his five books on the procession of the Holy Spirit, which I sent to Leo Allatius himself, to bring into the third volume of his Græcia orthodoxa; and so they, when sent, were lost, both to me and to the ecclesiastical cause. The last words I would render thus: ‘In the sense that the letter says [the Spirit] proceeds from the Son, it plainly explains it so that it is the same as to go forth through the Son.’ At length, too, [Veccus] to Constantine, book 4, p. 203 ff., where [he shows] very well that holy Maximus, as one concerned for both parties on the procession of the Holy Spirit, joined those words by softening them, in order to draw them to assent and calm the quarrel: [Greek:] ‘from which they showed themselves not to be making the Son the cause of the Spirit.’ They showed that they were not making the Son a cause of the Spirit: such as they seemed to themselves, from their own words and manner of speaking, to hold: a first [cause], that is, and such as the Father is; which had arisen for them from the dispute, and because the Latins accused them [the Greeks] of the heresy of the Monothelites; as the same Veccus says very well, p. 47, saying that he gathered this from Maximus’s letter; and anyone may readily notice that it was no otherwise in Photius and Cerularius, who turned private hatreds into a cause of the faith. In the excerpt from the letter which the Regius codex, cited above, says was written at Rome — the other, Roman [codex], which alone has it, joins it to the letter to Marinus, as if it were a part of it: καὶ μεθ᾽ ἕτερα (‘and after other things’) — how not at Rome,

sed Byzacii in Africa scripta esset. Ac num imperitus librarius Byzantium sibi pro Byzacio divinavit, ut eamdem epistolam, eodem loco scriptam sibi finxerit? Anastasius, quod non defloravit, nec habuit: nunquam omissurus sic illustre Romanæ fidei et Ecclesiæ, Petri privilegio, testimonium ac elogium. Nihil autem abhorret a Maximi aliis, quibus per occasionem Romanos laudat, eorumque in fide firmitatem: nusquam non fidei primatum et arcem Ecclesiasticæ communionis, in Romano Antistite ponens, a quo et absolutio ab hæresi impetranda sit, ac cujus arbitratu transigenda fidei negotia.
Movere possit, quod sex synodos numerat, cum sexta synodus Maximo jam consummato celebrata sit. Existimo sextam voluisse ipsam Romanam et Lateranensem Martino I pontifice, quæ pro sui celebritate sic quinque generalibus Maximo comnumerari potuit: qua vere Catholicis supremo judicio confossa hydra videretur, cui interfuisset aut communicasset, quidquid esset orthodoxum, reliquis per Orientem sedibus, excepta Hierosolymitana, Monothelitarum hæresi infectis: in qua perinde Sophronio auctore ea damnata fuerat, uti etiam a Joan. IV Romæ: sed non ea pompa et celebritate, qua a Martino e concilio Lateranensi, Maximo ipso illi incentore, cujus acta illustrissima exstarent, in quibus ventilata omnia, adductaque Scripturæ ac Patrum testimonia, quibus veritas catholica lucidissime statueretur, ac quidquid Monothelitarum furfuris esset, exsufflaretur, illorum etiam nominatim proscriptis capitibus: ut jam una Christianitatis tessera viderentur, in sancta una catholica, quo tantum sui desiderium per Orientem veris fidelibus consciverant, quantum Theodosius Gangrensis presbyter testatur in Hypomnestico. Nec ultra trahenda Maximi epistola ad Petrum illustrem, quam nobis servarit Anastasius in Collectaneis excerptam, unaque nobis Græce desideratur: cum alia dogmatica nobis exstent ad eumdem, in epistolis, quas sequentibus repræsento.
unplaced.en: […how not at Rome,] but written at Byzacium in Africa? And did an unskilled copyist, guessing Byzantium for Byzacium, invent for himself the same letter written in the same place? Anastasius, [for the part] he did not cull, he also did not have: he would never have omitted so illustrious a testimony and praise of the Roman faith and Church, of Peter’s privilege. Nor is it at all at odds with Maximus’s other letters, in which on occasion he praises the Romans and their firmness in the faith: everywhere placing the primacy of faith and the citadel of ecclesiastical communion in the Roman Bishop, from whom absolution from heresy is to be obtained and at whose judgment the business of the faith is to be settled. It might raise a difficulty that he counts six synods, when the sixth synod was held after Maximus had finished his course. I think he meant the Roman synod itself, the Lateran under Pope Martin I, which, for its renown, could be reckoned by Maximus with the five general councils: in which the hydra of the Monothelites was truly pierced by the supreme judgment of Catholics, [and] whoever had taken part or communicated, whatever was orthodox, while the other sees of the East, Jerusalem excepted, were infected with the Monothelite heresy: in which [the heresy] had been condemned likewise at the instigation of Sophronius, as also by John IV at Rome: but not with that pomp and renown with which it was condemned by Martin in the Lateran council, Maximus himself being its instigator, whose most illustrious acts survive, in which everything was debated, and testimonies of Scripture and the Fathers adduced, by which Catholic truth would be most clearly established, and whatever of the Monothelite chaff there was would be blown away, their leaders being proscribed by name, so that they might now appear a single badge of Christianity, in the one holy catholic [Church], for which true believers throughout the East had conceived as great a longing as Theodosius, priest of Gangra, bears witness in his Hypomnesticum. Nor is Maximus’s letter to Peter the Illustrious to be stretched further, which Anastasius preserved for us, excerpted, in his Collectanea, and which alone is lacking to us in Greek: since other dogmatic letters of his to the same man survive, among the letters which I reproduce in what follows.

Titulus apud Turr. paulo auctior; addit enim, Et quod Arius et Nestorius in theologia et incarnatione, contra atque Sabellius et Eutyches sentiant: quod ipsum indicat, unum hoc Maximum spectasse, ut contrarias has hæreses in Trinitate et Incarnatione contenderet, eisque fidem catholicam, ipsam illarum mediam, opponeret.

unplaced.en: From the Regius codex, collated with our Tilianus of St Hilary [Tiliano S. Hilarii] and with Dufresne’s, and with the Latin editions by Turrianus. Leontius is nearly the same. This very opuscule, short as it is, which survives in so many codices, is proof that it was once highly esteemed by many sons of the Catholic Church and served them as a sort of watchword against heretics who thought wrongly either about the Godhead or about the dispensation, that is the incarnation; nor is the heresy of Macedonius omitted, in our codex of St Hilary, whether Maximus himself inserted it or some zealous person added it to make the teaching fuller; I think the latter more likely, also because it is lacking everywhere in the other codices. I decided to reproduce it as well. The title in Turrianus is somewhat longer, for he adds ‘and that Arius and Nestorius think, in theology and in the incarnation, contrary to Sabellius and Eutyches’; which itself shows that Maximus had this one aim, to set these opposing heresies in the Trinity and the Incarnation against each other and to oppose to them the Catholic faith, which stands midway between them.

Ad illa verba Hilariani nostri cod. ἢ ταυτότητα οὐσιῶν, addo quæ necessaria sunt, ut sit plenus sensus, καὶ ἑτερότητα προσώπων, καὶ τὸ ἔμπαλιν. Aliter enim se res in Deo habet, aliter in Christo ac nobis, modoque opposito; quod utrumque propositum exponere Maximo, cum utrobique summa unio sit, altera essentialis seu natura, altera personalis ac subsistentia.

unplaced.en: ‘And how he affirms God.’ So our codex, not enclitically. Whoever wants τὸ πῶς (‘how’) said emphatically, and as with a certain wonder, I would not deny. So certainly I render with wonder what follows at once in the next number, ‘How the highest union has both sameness and otherness’ (Πῶς ἡ ἄκρα ἕνωσις); whereas Turrianus [renders it] by a question, ‘How does the highest union have both the same and the diverse?’ Maximus is not asking this but wondering, in divine things as in created; except that in divine matters the words ‘diversum’ and ‘diversitas’ are not quite apt, which Turrianus readily uses for ‘distinctum’ and ‘distinctio’, but [they mean] ‘other’, or ‘another’, or ‘differing’ and ‘difference’; since ‘diversus’ seems to bring in division; and so Ambrosius Calepinus renders ‘diversus’ as ‘separate’ (κεχωρισμένος): to which belongs Caesar’s phrase in the African War, ‘when they saw the Numidians scattered and fleeing in every direction’, and likewise Plautus in the Rudens, ‘thence each went his way, in different directions, home’. The more careful theologians would say ἑτερότης, if it were allowed, ‘alietas’; as also one person and another is said in divine matters: although ἕτερος properly regards two, ἄλλος more than two. To those words of our Hilarian codex, ἢ ταυτότητα οὐσιῶν, I add what is necessary to complete the sense, ‘and the otherness of persons, and the reverse’. For the matter stands one way in God, another in Christ and in us, and in the opposite manner; each proposition Maximus had to set out, since in both there is the highest union, the one essential or of nature, the other personal and of subsistence.

Missa hæc epistola, sive liber dogmaticus ad Stephanum Dorensem episcopum, fidei catholicæ cum archiepiscopo suo Sophronio adversus Monothelitas strenuum defensorem, inque eam rem ab eodem Romam missum, ubi orthodoxorum dogmatum fundamenta exsisterent, inquit idem Sophronius egregia illa suggestione, quæ exstat in concil. Later. sub Martino I, secretar. seu consult. 2. Cumque Maximus hanc Romam mittat, argumento est, sub exordium fere novi dogmatis missam esse, et cum solum edita esset Heracliana, seu magis Sergiana Ecthesis, in quam unam invehitur, nec Constantis Typus adhuc cusus esset, cujus illi Paulus, ipse in eo concilio damnatus, ac a Stephano exagitatus, auctor fuit. Tantæ ergo fidei in Stephano præcipuus incentor videatur Maximus; potuitque per eum sic Theodoro papæ innotescere, ut ei vices suas, et Conservatorium, ut vocabant, in Palæstina ac Hierosolymitana diœcesi concrederet: quo in munere suas strenue exsecutum partes, depositis, qui libellum pœnitentiæ non obtulissent, male promotis per Sergium Joppensem episcopis, ac qui fidei catholicæ scripto assensum non præbuissent, ipse in ea suggestione locuples testis exsistit. Quo et Romani antistitis mire elucet auctoritas, et sollicitudo Ecclesiarum, in causa præsertim fidei, qualis hic vertebatur, ubique terrarum vere orthodoxis spectatissima. Πρωτόθρονον Hierosolymitani throni seu sedis ac diœcesis haud obscure se Stephanus significat, sive id habebat suæ sedis privilegio, quæ esset prima et dignior usu ecclesiastico, cæteris post ipsam Hierosolymitanam sedem, sive etiam quia ipse senior episcopus erat, quomodo Africa primates suos agnoscebat; aut denique quod Conservatoriam a sede apostolica acceperat, vacante sede Hierosolymitana per Sophronii obitum. Hanc porro epistolam habuit etiam cod. Em. card. Barberini, ex qua plurima mutuata sexta synodus, præsertim Agatho in sua suggestione, ex cujus sensu peracta omnia in illo concilio, quæ ad fidei negotium spectabant, ut ejus triumphi præcipuæ partes Maximi fuisse videantur, ac gloria prostratæ Monothelitarum hæresis, tum Romæ Martino papa, tum Constantinopoli Agathone.
unplaced.anchorLine: Πνευματικὸς τόμος (α) καὶ δογματικὸς, ἀπεδεικνὺς
unplaced.en: (a) "Πνευματικὸς τόμος" (Spiritual Tome). This epistle, or dogmatic book, was sent to Stephen, bishop of Dora, as a stalwart defender of the catholic faith together with his archbishop Sophronius against the Monothelites, and was sent by him to Rome for that purpose, where the foundations of orthodox doctrines were to be found, as the same Sophronius says in that excellent suggestio which is extant in the Lateran council under Martin I, in the secretarium or consultation 2. Since Maximus sends it to Rome, it is evidence that it was composed near the beginning of the new doctrine, and when only the Heraclian, or rather Sergian, Ecthesis had been published, against which alone he inveighs, and Constans's Typos had not yet been struck, of which Paul, himself condemned in that council and attacked by Stephen, was the author. So Maximus seems the chief instigator of such great faith in Stephen; and through him he could thus become known to Pope Theodore, so that he entrusted to him his own vicarial powers and the Conservatorium, as they called it, in Palestine and the diocese of Jerusalem. In that office he vigorously carried out his duties: he deposed those who had not offered a petition of penance and had been wrongly promoted by Sergius of Joppa as bishops, and those who had not given assent to the written statement of the catholic faith; he himself stands as a reliable witness in that suggestio. By this the authority of the Roman pontiff shines out wonderfully, and the care of the Churches, especially in a cause of faith such as was being treated here, most conspicuous everywhere among the truly orthodox. Stephen indicates not obscurely that he is "Πρωτόθρονος" of the throne, or see and diocese, of Jerusalem, whether he had it by the privilege of his see, which was first and more worthy by ecclesiastical custom, the others coming after the see of Jerusalem itself; or also because he was himself the senior bishop, as Africa recognized its primates; or finally because he had received the Conservatoria from the apostolic see, the see of Jerusalem being vacant through Sophronius's death. This epistle, moreover, Cardinal Barberini's codex also contained, from which the sixth synod borrowed very much, especially Agatho in his suggestio, from whose sense everything in that council that concerned the matter of faith was carried out, so that the principal part of its triumph seems to have been Maximus's, and the glory of the overthrow of the Monothelite heresy, both at Rome under Pope Martin and at Constantinople under Agatho.

unplaced.en: ...[Agatho's reading] ἐστὶν δυνάμεως ('is of power'). So too in what follows Maximus used the word ἐξουσία: "that there is one will, one operation, according to one and the same authority going forth." In those passages ἐξουσία is more properly said of what we will and do γνωμικῶς (by choice and judgment) than of what we do φυσικῶς (naturally). The same appears a little later in the authority of Leo: ἐνεργεῖ ἐν ἑκατέρᾳ μορφῇ, which too is to be emended from the Latin to ἐνεργεῖ ἑκατέρα μορφή, 'each form acts'; it is so also in what follows, where the same authorities are briefly touched on. Perhaps Maximus wrote and rendered ἐνεργεῖ γὰρ ἐν ἑκατέρᾳ μορφῇ, which is in no way different in sense from the Latin, but rendered a little more elegantly. In that epistle of Leo, as Gerardus Vossius presented it in Greek, there are many variant readings, whatever care was applied to keep it pure, as it was issued by Leo, in the Churches everywhere, as the token of the true faith. Leo's very phrasing seemed far harsher to the confounders, as if favouring division in kind; yet it was needed all the more to crush their impiety. They would have had it milder, as it is represented here; and did one of them (or the copyist himself) wish to soften it thus? Surely not, I think, Maximus himself. The matter is proved by what is here, and by more in the acts of the sixth synod, their authorities.

unplaced.en: (i) "Ἀλλὰ αὐτοβουλίαν." I emend, from Sophronius's Synodica, to ταυτοβουλίαν (sameness of will); for this is ἓν θέλημα (one will), which Maximus himself explains. So Sophronius says the mystery of Christ is explained by Nestorius as ἰσοτιμίᾳ, ταυτοβουλίᾳ: by an equal sharing of honour, by the same will, etc. So also in the following treatise on the same subject: "from which he also establishes the ταυτοβουλίαν, or rather the πολυβουλίαν, to speak more fittingly." And you rightly see this, ταυτοβουλίαν, πολυβουλίαν: that Nestorius's one will is one only in affection or habit, relatively (σχετικῶς); but in fact, in nature and person, it is manifold for him, as things stand in friendship, in which we are called one and the same.

unplaced.en: Ὅροι ἑνώσεων (Definitions of unions). Turrianus has this short treatise almost last, though not complete; the Roman Greek codex appended it to the above. The union which he places first is that κατ᾽ οὐσίαν, which we must take as distinct from the one following, which is ἡ καθ᾽ ὑπόστασιν; and he sets out the conditions of both more fully at the end: namely, that the union according to essence is in diverse hypostases, that is persons and individuals, while that according to hypostasis is in diverse substances or natures. Cyril and other Fathers, however, call the union in Christ itself essential and natural, hypostatic, as being true, and to distinguish it from the relational union of Nestorius, that is, one standing in affection alone, such as is in the saints by grace. 'Hypostases of individuals': not quite aptly Turrianus, in that Maximus [says] ἐπὶ τῶν ὑποστάσεων, that is, of individuals, unless his codex read otherwise, and I think it certainly read otherwise, namely ἐπὶ τῶν ὑποστάσεων, τῶν ἀτόμων, which he thought he should render as it ought to have been rendered: In hypostases, which are individuals; a mode of speaking very familiar to the Greeks, and to Maximus among them. In what follows he seems to have had ὡς ἐπὶ ψυχῆς καὶ σώματος (as in the case of soul and body), which is also clearer, and I gladly follow it.

Qui de hara Calvini Ministellus in Septimania tentavit haud ita pridem Nestorium levare, Cyrillo detrahere, is suas in se contineat tenebras, nec orci novam fuliginem (cui satis sit Calvinianus candor hactenus Christianissimo orbe tantum non repressus) in claram ejus pubem, celebri orbis Lycæo procul aspergat.

unplaced.en: Ἡ κατὰ σχέσιν (the union by relation). Turrianus renders it 'according to habit', not rendering what follows, ὡς ἐπὶ τῶν γνωμῶν (as in the case of judgements); which it was easy for him to render, and from these to learn more thoroughly, or to explain, the force of κατὰ σχέσιν, according to Maximus's mind and that of the theologians against Nestorius. So it is the union which is through affection, by free will and choice, when many through agreement are of one opinion, one mind, one will: Εἷς ἓν θέλημα, 'that there be one will', not as Turrianus renders it, 'that there be one in wills'. This impure and Jewish doctrine of Nestorius, against whom no Catholic should be too indulgent, he brings in as a metaphysical evil rather than as most wicked blasphemy against the Son of God, overturning the whole mystery of the dispensation. Let him who of late, the little minister from the Calvinist brood in Septimania, tried to lighten Nestorius and to disparage Cyril, keep his own darkness within himself, and not sprinkle a new soot of hell (for whom the Calvinist candour, hitherto scarcely restrained in the most Christian world, should suffice) upon the clear face of the famous Lyceum of the world.

unplaced.en: "Τοῦ τῆς ἀναστάσεως φερωνύμως" (of him who is rightly named from the Resurrection). Out of these he promised also a fragment of the Diaitetes, from book 4 of that work, when he was about to publish five orations of Anastasius on the right doctrines of the faith; he does not seem to have kept his promise.

unplaced.en: "Δέος οὖν πολλὰ βαίνειν." This is plainly an error of the scribe. Anastasius, who renders it rather harshly, 'Timor ergo est opinari' (so it is fear to suppose), points to Maximus's letter as with a finger; namely, that he wrote 'Δέος οὖν ἐπιβάλλειν', or 'ἐπιβαλεῖν', which can also be rendered 'to feel, to understand, to suppose' at times; but the more apt, and more usual, sense of this word here is 'to add, to put under'. In this way the Latins at Rome, Maximus says, did not write the word 'one' in the letter, though it stands in the Greek; and so it is a spurious word, 'inserted' (ἐπιβεβλημένην), added by their fraud, who sought support for their novelty in the authority of so great a see: since especially in what was written so obscurely and simply, there seems no lack of occasion for inserting that word, and for seizing the whole letter for themselves, as though Honorius had in fact agreed with Sergius. And hence perhaps his summons and the pledge left at Rome in the end, lest, while it could not be sufficiently cleared, the first See itself might seem to contract some stain through his defence in Honorius's successors, men indeed as much the more distinguished for zeal of faith as Honorius, or at least by a milder effort in this regard, from his very origin, seemed to have obscured himself.

Libens Maximus scribit, his, qui Romanæ diœcesis erant; vel qui paulo remotiores ab urbe Constantinopolitana liberius et doceri fidem, et docere poterant, in ea urbe potissimum, longa præsulum Monothelitarum serie exagitatam ac pene excisam, donec tandem per Seniorem Romam, novæ fidei lux nova affulsit: nec tamen animorum omnem rancorem, etiam ei Honorio litans, eximere potuit, quin se ille brevi post explicaverit, in eo sacerdotum cœtu, qui iterum in Palatii Trullo, Justiniano II imperatore, convenientes, per absentiam aliarum omnium sedium patriarchalium, canones edidere, nec paucos apostolicæ sedi injurios; quo ausu schismati radicem posuere; ut bene Matthæus Caryophilus archiepiscopus Iconiensis, vir Græcorum catholicissimus, in Confutatione Nili Thessalon. De primatu papæ. Placetque illa ejus observatio: In summa, quidquid Orientales in conciliis egerunt clam papa, non sacris conciliis tribuenda sunt, sed artificiosis quorumdam machinamentis. De Honorio vero, Non ferebant quatuor Constantinopolitanos patriarchas anathematizari ut hæreticos Monothelitas, et non inseri Honorium Romanum. Idque adeo sit, quod ait Adrianus papa in viii synodo act. 7, dictum anathema Honorio post mortem ab Orientalibus, ὅτι ἐπὶ αἱρέσει κατηγορήθη· nec tamen sententiam ferre quemquam patriarcharum aut præsulum potuisse, εἰ μὴ ἡ τῆς αὐτῆς πρώτης καθέδρας αὐθεντία συνήνεσεν ἐπὶ τούτῳ. Reddebat Radd., Nisi ejusdem primariæ sedis accedente ad eam rem auctoritate. Tulisse itaque hanc injuriam Romanam Ecclesiam hæc significant, ut vel ea exulceratos Orientalium animos patriarcharum maxime ex nomine proscriptione e synodo Lateranensi, quovis modo liniret; uniusque periculo capitis, tot annorum schisma sopiret, ac Christi gregis tantam sibi partem, sicque illustrem (Senior Roma, novam; mater, filiam) adjungeret. Hæc Honorii antiquis […]ota defensio; hæc probata; hæc incolumis per tot sæcula, ante novitiam Sirleti ac sequacium cusam, steterat, stetitque ac stabit; ut sibi unius veritatis candor ecclesiasticis probe fultus monumentis, non conjectura nutans, semper sufficit: uno hoc Ecclesia feliciter vincit, nec ullam τ[…]ῖς ἔξω sua traducendi copiam facit; quin eorum imminet jugulo, hac vere armatura velut acies ordinata, illis terribilis
unplaced.en: [Continuation of note (e) on 'Mazara'.] ...of coastal Sicily, on the southern shore between Thermae. Philippus Ferrarius. Maximus writes it with pleasure, for those who were of the Roman diocese; or who, being a little farther from the city of Constantinople, were freer both to be taught the faith and able to teach it, in that city above all, which had been long harassed by a series of Monothelite prelates and almost cut down, until at last through Elder Rome a new light of faith shone upon it; yet he could not remove all rancour of mind, even in pleasing Honorius, but that he explained himself shortly after, in that assembly of priests who, meeting again in the Trullan hall of the Palace under the emperor Justinian II, in the absence of all the other patriarchal sees, issued canons, and not a few injurious to the apostolic see; by which daring act they laid the root of schism; as Matthaeus Caryophilus, archbishop of Iconium, a most Catholic man among the Greeks, rightly observes in his Confutation of Nilus of Thessalonica, On the primacy of the pope. And that observation of his is pleasing: 'In sum, whatever the Orientals did in councils without the pope is not to be attributed to the sacred councils, but to the artificial contrivances of certain men.' And of Honorius: 'They would not bear that four Constantinopolitan patriarchs be anathematized as Monothelite heretics, and that Honorius of Rome not be inserted.' And this is so, as Pope Adrian says in the eighth synod, act 7, that anathema was spoken against Honorius after death by the Orientals, 'because he was accused of heresy'; yet that no one of the patriarchs or prelates could pass sentence, unless the authority of the same first see agreed to it. Raddus rendered it: 'unless with the authority of the same primary see added to the matter.' That the Roman Church bore this injury these things signify: that she might soothe the embittered minds of the Orientals, chiefly by the proscription of the patriarchs by name in the Lateran synod; and by the risk of one head lull to sleep the schism of so many years, and join to herself so great a part of Christ's flock, and so an illustrious one (Elder Rome adding the new; the mother, the daughter). This defence of Honorius, known to the ancients [word blotted]; this was approved; this stood unharmed through so many centuries, before the novelty of Sirletus and his followers, stood and stands; so that the candour of one truth, well supported by ecclesiastical monuments, not wavering on conjecture, always suffices: by this one thing the Church happily conquers, and allows no opportunity of traducing her to those outside; nay, she hangs over their throat with this armature, like a battle-line drawn up, terrible to them.

Exemplum istud quod adhibet τοῦ ἐνυποστάτου, paulo φυσικώτερον est. Ita sane in naturalibus, hypostasis ex imperfectis substantiis conflatur, ex quibus unum totum ac per se exsistens consurgit: in Christo autem utraque perfecta natura est; unde nec unum totum ut natura ex eis conflatur, sed unus perfectus Deus, perfectus homo in utraque exsistit; ipsasque non hypostases, sed ἐνυπόστατα alibi Maximus admittit. Hic vero quod ponit exemplum, de imperfecto quod perfecto utitur unione secundum confusionem, hoc forte velit. Partes, quæ sic accedunt perfecto, ex illa imperfecti cum eo mistione et confusione, ut sic ἐνυπόστατα esse, quæ vere in hypostasi cui adveniunt, exsistant, non ut accidentia, sed ut quid substantiale, nec extra hypostasim, etsi non sint ipsa hypostasis, quæ est totius ratio, ac per se seorsum a quocunque alio, exsistentis. Paulo post τὸ ἐνυπόστατον, ad ipsa trahit communia accidentia seu adventitia, quæ et ipsa in hypostasi exsistant: sed id remotius est, quod illa esse valde debile et secundum quid in ea habeant. Sequentia, excerpta potius sunt, ad sequentem usque epistolam ad Constantinum Sacellarium, quam justa aliqua lucubratio vel epistola; cumque ipsius Maximi nomine prænotati loci afferantur, conjectura sit ejus studiosum aliquem hæc potius quam ipsum Maximum digessisse; vel si primum Maximus digessit adversus Severianos et Monothelitas, sic illi digesta alius auxerit, uti fere aliqui exsistimant de quæst. ad Antiochum Athanasii nomine, deque Anastasii Sinaitæ in Scripturam, aliis Nicæni.
unplaced.anchorLine: τουτέστι, τὸ μὴ ἐξ ἀτελῶν (h) μερῶν εἰς ἕν τι συνελ-
unplaced.en: On 'not from imperfect [parts]': Greek terms and the senses of words vary, and this causes difficulty in theology and ensnares the unwary, as Maximus himself sometimes warns. The example he uses of 'enhypostaton' is rather natural. Thus in natural things a hypostasis is compounded from imperfect substances, out of which one whole, self-existing thing arises; but in Christ each nature is perfect, so that neither is one whole formed from them as a nature, but one perfect God, perfect man, exists in both; and Maximus elsewhere admits them to be 'enhypostata', not hypostases. Here, however, the example he sets down, of the imperfect that is used by the perfect by union according to confusion, he perhaps means this: parts that thus join the perfect, from the mixture and confusion of the imperfect with it, so as to be enhypostata, which exist truly in the hypostasis to which they come, not as accidents but as something substantial, and not outside the hypostasis, though they are not the hypostasis itself, which is that of the whole and exists separately by itself from anything else. A little later he draws 'enhypostaton' to the common accidents or adventitious things, which also exist in the hypostasis; but that is more remote, since they have it only very weakly and in a qualified way. What follows is rather excerpts, as far as the next letter to Constantine the Sacellarius, than a proper treatise or letter; and since the passages are cited under Maximus's name, the conjecture is that some student composed these rather than Maximus himself, or, if Maximus first composed them against the Severians and Monothelites, that another enlarged his compilations, as some commonly suppose of the question to Antiochus under Athanasius's name, and of Anastasius of Sinai on Scripture, and others of the Nicene.
